planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Compacta is one of the most widely planted Japanese holly cultivars in the South, valued as a dense, easy-care boxwood substitute.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Compacta is a longtime standard Japanese holly cultivar valued for dense, fine-textured, small dark-green leaves and a naturally rounded, mounding habit that stays tidy with only light shearing, making it one of the most commonly planted boxwood substitutes across the humid South. It tolerates shearing into a formal hedge or foundation mass just as well as it looks left in its natural rounded form, and its small black fruit is of minor ornamental interest compared to red-berried hollies. Compacta adapts to a range of soil conditions but performs best with consistent moisture, and it holds up far better than boxwood to the fungal blights common in warm, humid Gulf South summers. Prune in late winter or right after the spring flush if a more formal shape is wanted.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Ilex crenata Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Japanese Holly as a Boxwood Alternative
University of Georgia Extension — Holly Selection Guide

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Helleri is one of the most compact and slowest-growing Japanese holly cultivars, ideal for a very low, tidy edge or foundation planting.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Helleri is a slow-growing, dwarf Japanese holly cultivar that stays under 3 feet, among the smallest commonly available selections, forming a dense, fine-textured mound of small dark-green leaves that reads much like dwarf boxwood without boxwood's disease problems in humid climates. Its low, tidy habit needs very little pruning to maintain, making it a favorite for low edging, foundation plantings under windows, and formal parterre-style beds where a very compact evergreen is needed. It tolerates shearing well if a crisper formal line is wanted. Consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil keep it looking its best, though established plants handle brief dry spells without lasting damage.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Ilex crenata Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Japanese Holly as a Boxwood Alternative
University of Georgia Extension — Holly Selection Guide

common_name: Duke Gardens Holly (Low Spreading Japanese Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Duke Gardens spreads wider than it grows tall, useful for a low, informal mass planting or foundation hedge.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Duke Gardens is a low, wide-spreading Japanese holly cultivar, named for the Duke Gardens in North Carolina where it was selected, with fine-textured, small dark-green leaves on arching branches that spread outward faster than the plant grows upward. Its low, billowing habit suits mass plantings, informal low hedges, and foundation plantings where a spreading rather than mounding or upright form is wanted. It shears well for a tidier, more formal line but also looks attractive left to its natural spreading habit. As with other Japanese holly cultivars, it tolerates the humid Gulf South climate far better than boxwood, with good resistance to the fungal blights that trouble boxwood, and performs best with consistent moisture in well-drained, acidic soil.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Ilex crenata Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Japanese Holly as a Boxwood Alternative
University of Georgia Extension — Holly Selection Guide

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; O'Spring is grown mainly for its variegated foliage rather than for berries, since it rarely fruits heavily.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. O'Spring is a Chinese holly cultivar grown chiefly for its bright, cheerful foliage — spiny, glossy leaves broadly margined in creamy yellow around a gray-green center — that brightens a shaded corner or mixed border year-round even without significant berry production. Its moderate, well-branched size fits a foundation planting, informal hedge, or mixed shrub border, and the variegated leaves make it a strong textural and color contrast against solid dark-green companions. Like other Chinese hollies it is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established, with very few pest or disease problems. Prune, if needed, in late winter to shape, since it tolerates shearing well but also looks attractive left to its natural upright form.

common_name: Center Stage White Crapemyrtle (Black-Foliage White-Flowered Compact Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Center Stage White is part of the same near-black-foliage Proven Winners series as Center Stage Red, on a compact 10-12 foot form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Center Stage White pairs near-black foliage with clean white flower clusters, giving especially crisp, high-contrast color for a crapemyrtle series bred by Spring Meadow Nursery for dramatic dark foliage. Bred for good disease resistance, it holds its dark leaf color through a humid Gulf South summer, and its compact 10-12 foot mature size fits more easily into a residential landscape than older, larger crapemyrtle varieties. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural vase-shaped form rather than topping it back hard.

common_name: Center Stage Coral Crapemyrtle (Black-Foliage Coral-Flowered Compact Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Center Stage Coral shares the near-black foliage of its Center Stage series siblings with warm coral-pink flowers, on a compact 10-12 foot form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Center Stage Coral bears warm coral-pink flower clusters set off dramatically against near-black foliage, part of the Spring Meadow Nursery series bred for season-long dark leaf color alongside strong disease resistance. It holds its foliage color well through humid Gulf South summers, and its compact 10-12 foot mature size fits more readily into a residential landscape than older, larger crapemyrtle varieties that need constant size control. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood rather than topping the plant back hard, which sacrifices its natural vase-shaped form.
